_note: TPO6 리포트 우선순위(강의 Main Idea · Speaker's Purpose · 리스닝 근거 검증)용 Listening 문제. 스크립트는 모두 새로 작성 — 원본 문장·정답을 재사용하지 않음.

lines.t: Listen to a talk in an urban planning class.

Cities have tried many ways to deal with traffic, and today I want to sort them into three broad strategies. The first strategy is to build more road space: wider highways, new bypasses. The problem is something called induced demand. When you add lanes, driving becomes easier, so more people drive, and within a few years the new lanes are just as crowded. The second strategy is pricing. London, for example, charges drivers a fee to enter the city center during busy hours. Fewer people drive in, and the money goes to public transport. The third strategy is to change land use, so that homes, shops, and offices are close together and people simply don't need to drive as far. By the way, this is also why some cities have started planting more trees along streets, which keeps sidewalks cooler in summer. So: supply, price, and distance. Keep those three in mind for the reading.
Listen to a talk on an astronomy podcast.

Planets around other stars are far too faint to see directly, so astronomers detect them indirectly. Let me describe the two most productive methods. The transit method watches a star's brightness. If a planet passes in front of the star, the star dims very slightly, and if that dimming repeats at regular intervals, we've probably found a planet. The size of the dip tells us how big the planet is. The second approach, the wobble method, looks for motion. A planet's gravity pulls on its star, so the star moves back and forth a tiny bit. That motion shifts the color of the star's light, and from that shift we can estimate the planet's mass. Each method has blind spots, which is why the most reliable discoveries are confirmed by both. Oh, and the first planet around a sun-like star was announced in 1995, which surprised many researchers at the time.
Listen to an announcement on a university radio station.

Attention, students. Starting next Monday, the group study rooms on the third floor of Hartley Library will require a reservation. You can book a room for up to two hours through the library's online system, and you'll need your student number to do it. Rooms that are not claimed within fifteen minutes of the booking time will be released to other students. The first-floor reading room will stay open on a walk-in basis, as always. And a quick reminder: the library café now opens at seven, an hour earlier than before.
Listen to a talk in a biology class.

Camouflage isn't only about matching the background. One important type is called disruptive coloration. Bold stripes or patches break up the outline of an animal's body, so a predator can't easily tell where the animal begins and ends. Think about a zebra in a moving herd. The stripes of many animals blend together, and a lion has trouble picking out a single target. Another type is countershading. Many fish are dark on top and pale underneath. Seen from above, the dark back matches the deep water; seen from below, the pale belly matches the bright surface. It's a bit like a stage designer who lights a set so that the edges of objects disappear. Some animals, like the cuttlefish, can even change their patterns within seconds.
Listen to a talk in an economics class.

Every choice has a hidden price. Economists call it opportunity cost: the value of the best alternative you give up. Say you have a free Saturday. You could work a shift and earn eighty dollars, or you could go hiking with friends. If you go hiking, the hike isn't free. Its opportunity cost is the eighty dollars you didn't earn. Businesses face the same problem. A bakery that uses its oven for bread can't use that oven, at that hour, for cakes. Opportunity cost is like the road not taken in a journey. You never see it on the map of where you went, but it shaped every turn. That's why good decisions compare options, not just prices.
Listen to a talk in an architecture class.

Medieval builders wanted cathedrals with very high walls and huge windows, to fill the interior with light. But a tall stone wall with big holes in it is weak. The heavy stone roof pushes the top of the wall outward, and the wall can collapse. Their solution was the flying buttress, an arm of stone built outside the wall that leans against it and carries that outward push down to the ground. Imagine a person leaning a hand against a wobbly bookcase to keep it upright. With the buttresses taking the load, the walls themselves no longer had to be thick, and builders could fill them with stained glass. Notre-Dame in Paris is a well-known example, and its buttresses were added partly because cracks appeared in the walls.
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

In one study on sleep and memory, volunteers learned a list of word pairs in the evening. Half of them then slept normally, and half stayed awake through the night in the lab. What the volunteers didn't know was that they would be tested again on the same word pairs the next morning. They thought the study was about mood. The group that slept remembered noticeably more pairs. Interestingly, the difference was largest for pairs the volunteers had found difficult. The researchers concluded that sleep may help strengthen new memories, especially weak ones. They were careful to say that the study doesn't tell us exactly how much sleep is needed. That's a question for future research.
Listen to a conversation between a student and an advisor.
I'd like to take the marine biology course next term, but the system says it's full.
That happens a lot with that course. Professor Okafor sometimes opens a few extra seats in the first week.
Should I just email her?
Let me check whether she's keeping a waiting list this year. If she is, I'll put your name on it. In the meantime, register for a backup course so you don't fall below full-time status.
Okay. I'll sign up for introductory geology, then.
Listen to a talk in an ecology class.

Let's look at an invasive plant called garlic mustard, which arrived in North America from Europe. Garlic mustard releases chemicals into the soil. These chemicals harm certain fungi that live on the roots of native trees. Those fungi help the trees absorb water and nutrients. So when the fungi decline, young native trees grow more slowly. Over time, the forest floor has fewer native seedlings and more garlic mustard. Notice that the plant doesn't attack the trees directly. It works through the soil. Some deer also avoid eating it, but researchers still disagree about how much that matters.
Listen to a talk in an environmental science class.

Today's topic is how city noise changes bird communication. Traffic noise is mostly low-pitched, so many city birds now sing at a higher pitch than birds of the same species in forests. Some also sing earlier in the morning, before rush hour starts. These changes help their songs be heard. Researchers have also noticed that city birds are often less afraid of people, though that is probably a separate effect.
Listen to a talk in a psychology class.

Studying the same material in several short sessions works better than one long session. This is called the spacing effect. Imagine watering a plant. A little water every day keeps it healthy, but a whole bucket once a week mostly runs out of the pot. Memory seems to work in a similar way.
Listen to a conversation.
Is the science museum open on Monday?
I'm not sure. I'll look at their website tonight and let you know.
